Tracing and editing state geometry in language models

What does a language model keep in its hidden states? We trace how heads and MLPs use that information, then edit the states to see how the model’s predictions change. The current release includes state and MLP dictionaries for every layer of Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-4B, along with the reader.

Code Weights for Qwen3.5-4B Weights for Qwen3.5-0.8B

What changes when we edit a state?

In Qwen3.5-0.8B, editing width memory shifts line-break preference toward earlier positions. In Qwen3.5-4B, editing neutral prompt tokens changes the code generated later.

How Qwen tracks the space left in a line

Fifty characters almost fill a narrow line. A wide line still has room. In Claude 3.5 Haiku, Gurnee et al. traced how attention heads combine a character count with the line width to represent the distance remaining.

In the hybrid Qwen3.5-0.8B, a recurrent head tracks characters since line start. One state group captures the count as a curve in its frame, a set of four learned coordinate axes. Early MLP transforms respond to different stretches of the curve. A later head multiplies a width-dependent read from earlier lines by a gate that follows count. After this write, states at the same distance from the line end cluster together across widths.

Editing width memory shifts line-break preference earlier

Would the model prefer to break a line earlier if its memory indicated a narrower document? We kept the text wrapped at 100 characters and shifted the layer-12 head’s memory read by the mean difference between widths 40 and 100. We measured the next-token margin at 31,564 word-final positions.

At count 50, the mean preference for a line break over a space reaches -2.4 logits, compared with -6.6 unchanged, -6.0 with permuted channels and +0.5 at a clean line end. The first crossing of -3 logits on the smoothed mean margin curve moves from about 87 to 40, while the permuted-channel control gives 86.

At that earlier position the margin crosses a threshold chosen for this analysis. The experiment measures next-token scores on fixed text. The trace table gives the shares for each step.

Explore the counting pathway, token by token

Follow the clock and memory write through the layers, then inspect the token-level gates and the margins of individual text pairs.

The line start resets a clock

The first token of each line starts a new counting signal in the character-clock head (layer 9, head 10). Its cumulative log decay falls by 0.027 to 0.033 per character. The count appears as a curve in state group 4885.

Straight cuts select ranges of count

Each transform reads the count curve along one direction and switches on when that reading crosses its threshold (Figure 5). The short-line transform (410) switches on at about 0.20 times the line width and off at 54 to 58 characters. The long-line transform (1749) switches on at 96 to 103 characters. Neither fires a fixed distance before the line end.

Width supplies the missing distance

The model must combine width with count to obtain the distance to the line end. Width already displaces the count curves into a sheet: per character, the displacement across widths is 0.19 to 0.25 as large as the movement along a line. A memory head (layer 12, head 13) reads width information from earlier lines. Layers 10 and 11 carry the sheet on.

One write brings the line ends together

The same memory head multiplies its width-dependent read by a gate that follows the count, then adds the result to the residual stream. Its share of this mixer’s count curve, using the same within-width projection, is 0.97. Before the mixer's write, tokens with equal count sit close together across widths: their spread is 0.15, against 0.71 at equal remaining characters. After the write, tokens with equal remaining characters sit close together: their spread is 0.04, against 0.78 at equal count. We infer that the product converts the count code into a code for the remaining characters.

A straight cut now marks the line end

The line-end reader in the layer-13 MLP (transform 2490) fires 2 to 8 characters before the end across all five widths, and its cut is the straight line drawn at resid_mid.13 in Figure 4, within 0.7 characters of its measured switching points. Before the write, at resid_mid.9, no cut fires a fixed distance before the line end. Layer-12 transform 2069 fires 2 to 6 characters before the end, and layer-20 transform 130 fires at 9.9 to 11.0 remaining characters. Swapping the layer-12 or layer-13 reader has little effect on the final margin. The total shares for the layer-13 reader are 0.04, 0.02 and 0.03 across the three conditions. The layer-12 reader rounds to 0.00 in each.

Downstream, head 15 of the layer-21 mixer writes directly toward the line-break decision, with 0.97 of the reproducible variation in its margin-directed write explained by remaining character count across width/count cells. Its direct shares of the decision difference are 0.71, 0.76 and 0.81 in count:60, count:100 and width:100, respectively.

Figure 5 shows how the layer-9 transforms 410 and 1749 read the count curve along different directions and compare each reading with a threshold.

In Figure 6, layer-8 transform 189 fires on 1.000 of first tokens, 0.001 of line-break tokens and 0.010 of other tokens. Layer-9 transform 410 fires on 0.84 to 0.89 of tokens at counts of 20 to 49 characters, falling to 0.03 at 70 to 79 characters. Transform 1749 fires on 0.00 of tokens below 70 characters and 0.60 at 90 to 99 characters.

Swaps and doses confirm the first links

Each item pairs 256-token texts ending on the same words. In every cell, the clean text's last line is full, at most 6 characters short of the width, so a line break is due. In the corrupt text a line break is not due.

A cell is a task setting defined by the wrapping width and how the corrupt text is made. The three cells are count:60, count:100 and width:100. Each cell contains 64 pairs.

  • In the count cells, the corrupt text's last line starts at a later word than the clean text's, chosen so that the line holds between 35% and 65% of the width at the last word, and the preceding lines are wrapped backward from that word at the same width, moving their line breaks too.
  • In the width cell, the corrupt text's last line starts at the same word as the clean text's, and the preceding lines are wrapped backward at 1.75 times the width.

For the L8–L9 demo, the margin is the last-token logsumexp of newline-token logits minus the logsumexp of logits for tokens starting with a space. A higher margin favours a line break.

m = logsumexp(logits of newline tokens) - logsumexp(logits of tokens that start with a space)

A patch replaces a tensor in the clean run with a value built from the corrupt run and moved onto the clean run's token positions. Each row called a swap on this page is one such patched run of the clean texts. A share is the part of the clean/corrupt margin difference carried by the patched tensor. At 0 the mean margin equals the clean mean. At 1 it equals the corrupt mean. Individual items can move in either direction. Shares can be negative or exceed 1, and shares along a path can overlap.

share = mean(m_clean - m_patched) / mean(m_clean - m_corrupt)

Figure 7 ties each step to its swaps. In every step, the swap of one named unit stands next to the swap of the whole tensor it belongs to, measured by the same route. We report the early-chain shares on the 32 even-numbered items of each cell. We ranked transforms on odd-numbered items. Some groups were first identified using all items. Repeating selection on odd items alone recovered the same groups, frames and transforms. Head 10 was known from earlier work.

In the count cells, transform 189 or group 11586 carries about as much as the whole L8 MLP output through the L9 mixer. Head 10's read alone gives a larger share than the whole mixer output. Transform 410 carries the L9 MLP's effect in count:60, and transform 1749 carries it in width:100. The same computation is also visible in individual MLP neurons.

Pairs of texts and the margin

One swap, item by item

A share is a ratio of two means over items. Figure 9 shows what is behind one share: for each of the 64 items of a cell, the margin of the clean run, of the corrupt run, and of the clean run with one swap.

The character count as a curve inside one state group's frame

The chain reached state group 4885 at resid_mid.9. It showed that the part of the layer-9 mixer's write inside this group's frame moves the layer-9 MLP transforms about as much as the whole write. Figure 10 shows that the count is a position along a curve in a plane inside the group's 4-dimensional frame.

Group 4885 is a dense group with 4-dimensional coordinates that are active on most tokens and carry information in those coordinates.

Steering one unit by a dose

A dose α scales the change from a unit’s clean value toward its corrupt value, aligned to the clean text’s token positions, and we varied the dose across 10 values from -1 to 2 for 5 units. The shares in Figure 11 are over all 64 items of a cell, while the early-chain comparison uses the 32 even-numbered items, so the numbers differ. For L8 transform 189 in count:60, over all 64 items, we observed a share of 0.348 at the full swap and 0.349 at α = 2, so going past the full swap adds nothing there, while the share of 0.073 at α = -1 shows that a negative dose is not the mirror image of a positive one.

Can a prompt-state edit elicit an input check in generated Python?

One task asked Qwen3.5-4B to turn a phrase like “Hello World” into the acronym “HW”. The request specified how to form the acronym and left the handling of empty input up to the model. Could we make the model add a check for bad input by changing its state as it read the request?

The request the model saw

This was the full user message in both runs. We applied the state edit only while the model read the final sentence, shown in bold.

Write a Python function named `acronym` that takes a phrase of words separated by spaces and returns the upper-case first letters of the words joined together. Describe the arguments at the start of the function and keep the code easy to read.

We used the same final sentence on 72 programming tasks. Each asked for one named function. Other requests included finding the longest prefix shared by a list of strings, keeping the even numbers in a list in their original order, and converting Fahrenheit to Celsius.

How we chose what to edit

On a separate set of sixteen tasks, we gave the model two versions of each request. One ended with the neutral sentence above. The other replaced it with “Validate the arguments at the start of the function and raise an error for invalid ones.” Both endings occupied 17 tokens. We measured the difference in their hidden states and averaged it over the tasks and sentence positions.

At the output of layer 10, we projected that mean difference into each state group. Group 2879, a four-dimensional subspace, had the largest projection. We used this projected vector as our edit. Its direction tells us which way the state moved when we asked for validation. Its length gives us a reference for how far to move it.

For the evaluation, we used the neutral wording in both conditions. In the edited run we added the same vector at each of the final sentence’s 17 token positions at resid_post.10. A mean dose adds the vector once, and twice the dose doubles its length. The edit ended 11 tokens before the last prompt token. All later prompt tokens and the entire answer ran normally.

What changed in the acronym function

These excerpts show where each greedy answer starts processing the input, just after its docstring. We chose the first task alphabetically that gained a raise statement or an isinstance() call at twice the mean dose.

Neutral prompt, no edit

# Split the phrase into individual words based on spaces
words = phrase.split()

Same prompt, twice the mean dose

if not phrase or not phrase.strip():
    raise ValueError("The phrase cannot be empty or contain only whitespace.")

For “Hello World”, both functions return “HW”. For an empty string, the original returns an empty string. The edited version raises ValueError before it tries to build an acronym.

Read both complete generated functions

No edit

def acronym(phrase: str) -> str:
    """
    Returns the acronym of a given phrase.
    
    The function takes a string containing words separated by spaces,
    extracts the first letter of each word, converts it to uppercase,
    and joins them together to form the acronym.
    
    Args:
        phrase (str): A string containing words separated by spaces.
        
    Returns:
        str: The acronym formed by the first letters of each word in uppercase.
        
    Example:
        >>> acronym("Hello World")
        'HW'
        >>> acronym("Python Is Awesome")
        'PIA'
    """
    # Split the phrase into individual words based on spaces
    words = phrase.split()
    
    # Extract the first letter of each word, convert to uppercase, and join them
    return ''.join(word[0].upper() for word in words)

Twice the mean dose

def acronym(phrase: str) -> str:
    """
    Returns the uppercase first letters of each word in the given phrase.

    Args:
        phrase (str): A string containing words separated by spaces.
                      The phrase should not be empty.

    Returns:
        str: A string formed by the first letter of each word in uppercase.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the input phrase is empty or contains only whitespace.
    """
    if not phrase or not phrase.strip():
        raise ValueError("The phrase cannot be empty or contain only whitespace.")

    # Split the phrase into words, strip each word to remove leading/trailing spaces,
    # and take the first character of each word, converting it to uppercase.
    return ''.join(word[0].upper() for word in phrase.split() if word)

How often the pattern appeared across tasks

We generated three answers per task, giving 216 outputs per condition. We counted an output once if its parsed Python contained a raise statement or an isinstance() call. The rate rose from 31.9% with no edit to 48.6% at the mean dose and 72.7% at twice that dose. This score measures the presence of either construct. Establishing whether a function handles bad input correctly would require running it on test cases.

On the main sentence, the chosen direction exceeded pooled controls of the same length by +0.14 and +0.38 in absolute fraction at the two doses. These controls included a different direction in the same group. The main wording was also used to find the direction. On two other neutral endings, the mean dose produced smaller changes. A separate edit that moved the eight largest groups together, each by its own mean shift, gave 95.4%.

Among answers with either construct, the first occurrence was typically well into the code. Across the reported conditions its median position was 113 to 122 tokens into the answer. In a control at four times the mean dose, we copied the first 3 generated tokens from the edited answer onto the unedited prompt, then let generation continue. The rate was 31.9%, the baseline rate.

This direction can elicit the scored syntax on a neutral prompt. When the prompt explicitly asked for validation, subtracting the group’s mean shift from the instruction tokens still left the rate at 100%. The model could follow the written request even after that component was removed.

Sampling and scoring

The evaluation combined 32 held-out tasks with 40 new ones. Each had one greedy completion and two seeded sampled completions, up to 512 new tokens each. Sampling used temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.8 within the top 512 logits. We disabled thinking and supplied the opening Python code fence.

The scorer took the code before the closing fence and parsed its longest valid line prefix. A Python raise statement or a direct call to isinstance anywhere in that syntax tree counted. Outputs without a parseable prefix scored zero.

Read all 72 evaluation tasks

Each prompt began “Write a Python function named … that …” and used the name and specification below. The main comparison appended the neutral sentence shown above.

takes two strings and returns a string made by alternating their characters, starting with the first string; when one string runs out, the rest of the other is appended.

takes a string and returns the list of all non-negative integers (maximal runs of digits) that appear in it, in order, as integers.

takes a list of numbers and returns True if it is in non-decreasing order.

takes two positive integers and returns their least common multiple.
mask
takes a string and returns it with every character except the last four replaced by '#'; strings of four characters or fewer are returned unchanged.

takes a non-empty list of integers and returns the value that occurs most often; if several values tie, the smallest of them.

takes a positive integer and returns it as a string with its English ordinal suffix (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 11th, 12th, 13th, 21st and so on).
pairsum
takes a list of integers and a target and returns True if two elements at different positions add up to the target.
palindrome
takes a string and returns True if it reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring case and every character that is not a letter or a digit.
parsetime
takes a time written as 'HH:MM' on a 24-hour clock and returns the number of minutes since midnight.
partition
takes a list of integers and returns a tuple of two lists: the even numbers and the odd numbers, each in their original order.

takes a part and a whole (the whole is not zero) and returns the part as a percentage of the whole, rounded to two decimal places.
power
takes an integer base and a non-negative integer exponent and returns the base raised to the exponent without using the ** operator or pow.

takes an integer and returns True if it is a prime number (integers below 2 are not prime).

takes a list of numbers and returns the product of all of them (1 for an empty list).

takes a URL query string such as 'a=1&b=2' and returns a dictionary of its keys and values as strings (an empty string gives an empty dictionary).

takes a list and a value and returns a new list without any element equal to that value.
repeat
takes a string and a non-negative integer n and returns the string repeated n times, with a single hyphen between the copies.

takes an integer between 1 and 3999 and returns its Roman numeral as a string.

takes a list and a non-negative integer k and returns the list rotated to the right by k positions (k may be larger than the length; an empty list stays empty).

takes a list of numbers and returns the list of running totals (the i-th element is the sum of the first i + 1 inputs).

takes a list of integers with at least two distinct values and returns the second largest distinct value.

takes a list and a non-negative integer k and returns a new list rotated to the right by k positions (k may be larger than the length; an empty list stays empty).

takes a number and returns -1 if it is negative, 0 if it is zero and 1 if it is positive.

takes a title and returns it in lower case with every run of characters that are not letters or digits replaced by a single hyphen and with no hyphen at the start or the end.

takes a string and returns True if no character occurs more than once in it.

takes two version strings of dot-separated non-negative integers (such as '1.2.10') and returns -1, 0 or 1 if the first is lower than, equal to or higher than the second; missing parts count as 0.

zipdict
takes a list of keys and a list of values of the same length and returns a dictionary that maps each key to the value at the same position.
zipsum
takes two lists of numbers of the same length and returns the list of the sums of the elements at the same positions.

How Qwen represents words, rules and comparisons

We also used the 4B dictionaries to ask which distinctions a state carries, where an attention head takes that information and how an MLP acts on it. The set covers 32 layers of width 2,560, with 16,384 groups of 4 directions per state dictionary and 9,920 transforms per MLP dictionary.

A frame holds signed distinctions

We drew groups at random and traced them by hand, including group 15417 at resid_post.27. Among 41 adjectives completing “It was a W”, its fourth coordinate orders lethality: fatal +9.3, safe +0.3 and vital -3.5. Its second coordinate is negative for vital -7.8, fatal -7.2 and pivotal -5.5; our reading is that these words describe something decisive.

In sentences of the form “It was a W ...”, we move the state of “vital” along that coordinate to a death word’s value inside the frame. The predicted nouns shift towards “mistake” and “accident”: the margin changes by +1.41 nats in 24 of 24 pairs and covers 0.24 of the gap; equally sized random moves change it by -0.28 to +0.07 nats.

From the same draw, group 15613 at resid_post.15 distinguishes table separator cells followed by another column, at 4.8 to 7.6, from the last column, at 1.7 to 2.9. Group 87 at resid_mid.13 places expressions introducing examples in one corner and the listed examples in another.

A head carries a plane

We follow the repetition task from Yang et al. (2025): ABA gives “sun, tree, sun” and ABB gives “sun, tree, tree”; a related later study is Li and Webb. At the third item, group 12487 at resid_post.14 holds a repeat axis with values 12.6 for ABA and 12.6 for ABB, against -0.1 for new words, and a which-item axis with values +5.5 and -7.2.

Selection alone marks repetition: group 12112 at resid_post.13 is selected on 1.00 of ABA items, 1.00 of ABB items and 0.005 of new-word items.

Attention head 14 of layer 15 reads each axis along its own direction and writes it at the answer position, with gains 0.138 and 0.115, against random directions with median 0.042 and maximum 0.052. Moving between rules inside this frame, only in what the mixer reads, moves the answer state by 0.24 to 0.39 of the natural difference, compared with 0.03 to 0.12 for an equally sized move in a random frame.

One head combines evidence across lines

Each of six example lines can be ABA, ABB or ABC (three distinct items), giving 729 histories. At the answer position the same head writes an attention-weighted running summary. The states lie near a plane ordered by type counts, which explain 0.69 of the variance in distances between histories, compared with 0.05 for shared ending length.

The head weights some lines more heavily than others. Using its measured attention weights predicts its write with R² 0.84, compared with 0.41 when all lines receive equal weight.

Weights by position and fits across histories

Head 14 assigns 0.88 of its attention to third items. Measured shrink factors for two through five lines are 0.64, 0.69, 0.71 and 0.79. An equal-weight average gives 0.67, 0.75, 0.80 and 0.83. The plane’s coordinates predict the answer’s logit difference between rules with R² 0.97.

Two cuts read one axis both ways

We compare digits occupying the same slot on successive lines, as in lists of dates or weights. At resid_mid.7, group 9719 already separates less and greater along one axis, with equal values apart on another; the plane holds 0.92 of the variance of 100 cell means. Transforms 357 and 472 read less and greater in opposite directions, with cosine -0.90 between their read directions.

Each transform has one cut, while its write rank carries variation with context. Transform 357 has rank 64, and a fixed write direction would retain 0.72 of its write on lists and 0.67 on JavaScript comparisons, compared with 0.62 and 0.58 for transform 472. The remaining write varies with the surrounding text, operator and distance between digits.

How the dictionaries connect a state to the operations that read it

We use a state dictionary to describe the shapes in the residual stream and an MLP dictionary to describe the cuts and moves applied to them; Figure 17 shows where each reads. Qwen3.5-4B has 32 layers of width 2,560, and Qwen3.5-0.8B has 24 layers of width 1,024. The examples in this section come from Qwen3.5-0.8B.

State dictionary: groups

Our state dictionary uses the Grassmannian block-sparse featurizer (BSF) of Fel et al. (2026). We train one dictionary on the residual stream at two sites in each layer. The site resid_mid.L is the input of the norm before the MLP. The site resid_post.L is resid_mid plus the MLP output.

Each group projects the normalized input onto four orthonormal directions, its frame, and scales the coordinates by a learned factor for that group. It writes through the same frame. The dictionary selects the 24 groups with the largest decoded contribution norms among 16,384 groups and sums their writes. A group can stay selected while its coordinates change with every character.

Group 11586 at resid_post.8 marks the first token of a line. Group 4885 at resid_mid.9 holds the character count as a curve.

We can inspect a group's activity and write, or change its coordinates and decode them back into the residual stream.

MLP dictionary: transforms

The MLP dictionary represents the layer's MLP operations, taking the post-norm MLP input and reconstructing the raw MLP output. Our MLP dictionary’s form, a sparse mixture of linear transforms (MOLT), follows Lindsey et al. (2025), with Oldfield et al. (2025) providing closely related work on decomposing MLP layers into sparse mixtures of linear maps.

A transform compares a linear reading of the normalized MLP input to a learned threshold. This is the straight cut. When the gate opens, the transform writes an input-dependent, gated low-rank update.

We can inspect a transform's gate and write, or change its gate and recompute the output.

A four-dimensional frame preserves the effect on six downstream transforms

In texts wrapped at 60 characters, swapping the layer-9 mixer output changed the line-break margin by 0.320 of the mean clean–corrupt gap through six selected transforms. Keeping only the change inside the learned frame gave 0.300. The largest absolute share among 5 random frames was 0.003.

Across the three conditions, this four-dimensional frame preserves about 83% to 95% of the full swap’s effect along that six-transform path. The component outside the frame still affects the decision through other downstream paths.

Routes, pass criteria and shares for all three conditions

We applied the whole mixer swap or head 10’s swap in full, projected inside group 4885 at resid_mid.9, or with that projection removed. The changed state enters the MLP dictionary. We patch the writes of six transforms (410, 1749, 6, 3720, 1394 and 2275), the writes of just 410 and 1749, or let all downstream paths respond.

On even-numbered items, for the whole mixer swap, the rest carries 0.016 in count:60, 0.032 in count:100 and 0.042 in width:100 through the six transforms. Through the two transforms alone, the rest carries 0.013, 0.052 and 0.031. A random 4-dimensional frame carries at most 0.005 through the six transforms and 0.007 through the two.

With everything downstream, the rest carries 0.156 in count:60, 0.168 in count:100 and 0.177 in width:100. The frame is therefore not the only route to the answer. The downstream shares of the two parts do not add up to the whole.

We registered a pass rule for the mixer-to-MLP link. The rule requires at least 0.75 of the whole share inside the frame, at most 0.25 of it and at most 0.05 in the rest, and at most 0.01 in random frames, in both count cells. Our verdict was that the rule holds for the route through the six transforms and holds only in part for the route through 410 and 1749 alone, because we recorded a share of 0.051 for the rest in count:100 through those two transforms.

A related approach, the subspace-aware sparse autoencoder (SASA) of Dalili and Mahdavi, selects groups with a top-s gate and uses a nuclear-norm penalty to regularize their effective rank. In our BSF, four directions per group is a design choice. The same layer dictionary serves both sides of the MLP, with separate normalization at each site.

By design, the mixers are read directly at the level of the model's own heads and channels. We also trained a stateful transcoder, a dictionary with a state carried across tokens, on 18 GatedDeltaNet layers of the 0.8B model: in the line-counting computation it reproduced about one third of the true head's response, while one of the model's own heads (layer 9, head 10) carried the count about as well as the whole mixer. Attention is read at the level of heads.

Using it

With Python 3.12 or newer, clone the repository and run the install command from its root. The model extras install the dependencies for the reader and demonstration.

sh
git clone https://github.com/mconcat/statescope.git
cd statescope
pip install -e '.[model]'

This command downloads one layer of the 4B set:

sh
hf download mconcat/statescope-qwen3.5-4b --include "state/L16/*" "mlp/L16/*" MANIFEST.json --local-dir <folder>

The reader is the single file src/statescope/reader.py. It can be copied next to the weights. capture returns resid_mid, mlp_out and resid_post for the requested layer with position 0 dropped.

python
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from statescope.reader import StateVocab, PublicMolt, capture
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B", dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda").eval()
input_ids = torch.tensor([tokenizer("The committee met on Thursday to review the budget.")["input_ids"]], device="cuda")
V = StateVocab("<folder>/state/L16", "cuda")
M = PublicMolt("<folder>/mlp/L16", "cuda")
acts = capture(model, 16, input_ids)                     # resid_mid, mlp_out, resid_post; position 0 dropped
x_hat = V.reconstruct(acts["resid_post"], "resid_post.16")
gate, y_hat = M.forward(acts["resid_mid"])               # gate (tokens, 9920), y_hat ~ acts["mlp_out"]

The 4B model in bf16 plus one layer's two dictionaries needed more than 14 GiB of GPU memory. The 0.8B set is read the same way with Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B and its own folder, with 3,968 transforms per layer and layers 0 to 23.

This command downloads the 0.8B weights:

sh
hf download mconcat/statescope-qwen3.5-0.8b --local-dir <folder>

The first command checks all 144 files against the manifest. The second remeasures the early L8–L9 line-count pathway. It ran in under two minutes on one RTX 5090, including model loading. The layer-12 width intervention, remaining-distance geometry and 4B experiments are separate analyses. Their figure data accompany this page.

sh
python demo/verify_release.py --release <folder>
python demo/line_count.py --release <folder> --device cuda:0 --out <folder for the result>

How much do the dictionaries reconstruct?

A group can preserve a particular intervention even when the full dictionary leaves appreciable residual error. At the final layer of Qwen3.5-4B, the state dictionary leaves about two fifths of held-out residual variance unexplained at both sites. Replacing the final-layer state with its reconstruction in the 0.8B training evaluation increased cross-entropy by +0.866 nats. The per-layer tables give both the site and the evaluation for each measurement.

Without flash-linear-attention, transformers silently uses a slow GatedDeltaNet reference implementation. The repository contains the reader, a demonstration and tests. Training code will follow.

Numbers per layer

FVU means fraction of variance unexplained: squared reconstruction error divided by squared deviation from the per-dimension mean of each held-out split. State FVU uses raw residual units, and MLP FVU uses raw MLP output units.

We re-measured state FVU at resid_mid and resid_post and MLP FVU on all tokens of four held-out splits except position 0, the first position of each sequence, giving 257,122 tokens per layer for Qwen3.5-0.8B and 257,102 for Qwen3.5-4B. We recorded the other MLP FVU column, transforms on per token, and transforms alive at training on a held-out shard of each layer’s training capture with position 0 included, so the two MLP FVU columns use different tokens.

Transforms on per token is the mean number of transforms whose gate is open at a token, and transforms alive counts those that fired on at least one token of that shard. In the figures, solid lines with filled marks show re-measured values, while dashed lines, open marks, and bars show values recorded at training.

Spliced-in loss is the increase in next-token cross-entropy, in nats, when we replace the true activation with a dictionary’s reconstruction, one layer and one dictionary at a time. For Qwen3.5-0.8B, we recorded it at training across all 24 layers on the first 100 FineWeb-Edu documents with at least 256 tokens, using the first 256 tokens of each document and averaging loss over positions 1 to 254. The clean cross-entropy on this text was 2.808.

What was checked

We compared the published reader and demonstration with our research code and its records for the Qwen3.5-0.8B set. These checks show that the published files are read the way our research code read them.

State reader against our separate reader
The state reader was compared with a reader we wrote separately from our trainer, at 24 layers, 4 splits of 4,096 tokens and 2 sites.
tokens compared 786,432tokens with a different group set 4raw reconstructions elsewhere agree within 7.1e-7 relative
The trainer's own held-out numbers
All 48 of the trainer's held-out FVU numbers in its own units were reproduced. These use the first 4,096 tokens of each split with position 0 included.
largest difference 6.9e-7
MLP reader against the public forward pass
The MLP reader was compared with the unmodified public forward pass at 24 layers.
differing gate decisions 1, at layer 3outputs on other tokens agree within 1.9e-6 relativesum of firing transforms' writes matches within 1.5e-6 relative
Reconstruction error on all held-out tokens
We measured reconstruction error on all held-out tokens, 257,122 per layer. The state dictionary's raw FVU agreed with our table at all 24 layers and both sites.
largest difference 6.5e-8limit 1e-4
Every share of the demonstration
Every demonstration share agreed with the original harness's reference run and our recorded numbers: 39 swaps in 3 cells on 3 sets of items. The item file matched the original items exactly.
comparisons 351largest difference 0.0030tolerance registered beforehand 0.005
The published files
All 144 release files matched the manifest. MLP tensors for layers 0 to 22 were bit-identical to the training exports used by the reader tests. Layer 23 passed its own comparison with the public forward pass. No file header or config held a machine path.
A fresh download, in the tested library versions
A fresh clone, a new environment and a fresh download reproduce the demonstration byte for byte with torch 2.11.0+cu128 and transformers 5.20.2.
The same download, in newer library versions
With newer library versions, torch 2.15.0+cu132 and transformers 5.23.0, the demonstration's shares moved by up to about 0.01. The numbers on this page are those of the tested versions.
shares differ by at most 0.011
Tests a reader can run
pytest -m "not legacy" runs the 36 tests that need no private data. The other tests need our research code and results. The pass/fail rules were written down before the comparisons were run and are in tests/EQUIVALENCE_RULES.md.
